opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the basic intuition is that digital information is just so much easier to work with than atoms. If your job is fundamentally about taking in bits, transforming them, and putting out bits, that's reading, writing, coding, analyzing, summarizing, then the whole loop can, in principle, happen inside a computer. These models are trained on huge amounts of digital text and code, so they're natively fluent in exactly the medium those professions operate in.

Compare that to anything physical. With robotics you have to deal with sensors, actuators, hardware that breaks, the messiness of the real world, safety, and the cost of manufacturing and deploying machines. Atoms are expensive and slow; bits are cheap and you can copy them. So I'd expect a pretty big asymmetry where the digital stuff moves first and much faster, and the physical stuff lags, maybe significantly.

I don't necessarily think of it as "jobs disappear," though. It's more like the nature of the work changes. A lot of these roles become more about supervision: you're directing a system, checking its outputs, setting up the problem well, and applying judgment where the model is still weak. The models are kind of jagged. They're superhuman at some things and make surprisingly dumb mistakes at others, so you still want a human in the loop who understands the domain. But the amount of leverage a single person has in a digital profession goes up a lot. Something that took a team might take one person with good tools. That's the part I find exciting, and also the part where I think things will shift quickest.

r001.rationale: The response says models are fluent in digital text and code and can work with bits, but does not frame AI as a third kind of manipulator alongside humans and conventional computers.

r002.rationale: It says digital work will move first and faster, while physical work will lag, potentially significantly.

r003.rationale: It says jobs do not necessarily disappear and work changes, but does not state that AI-driven changes alone leave open whether employment rises or falls.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention demand elasticity as a factor affecting employment.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the simplest way to put it is that these models are, at their core, machines that transform bits into bits. That's the whole thing. You feed them tokens, they produce tokens. And so the question of which jobs get touched first is really just a question of which jobs are already, in their day-to-day reality, mostly bits in and bits out.

If you look at a software engineer, or a radiologist reading scans, or a paralegal going through contracts, or an accountant, or a lot of what analysts and writers and call center workers do, the actual work product lives entirely inside a computer. The inputs are digital, the outputs are digital, the feedback loop is digital. There's no physical world in between that the model has to reach through. So the bottleneck to automating that work is purely a question of capability, and capability is the thing that's been improving on this very steep curve.

Contrast that with a plumber or an electrician or a nurse. There, even if the model perfectly understood what needed to happen, you still have to get atoms moved around in a messy, unstructured environment. Robotics is coming, I'm very bullish on it long term, but the hardware is a much slower, much more capital-intensive loop. You can't just deploy a new version to a million plumbers overnight the way you can push an update to a million text editors.

The other thing I'd add is that the digital professions are also the ones where we have the most data. The internet is basically a giant corpus of people doing knowledge work, and the models were trained on that. So it's not just that the interface is convenient, it's that the models already have this enormous prior over what that work looks like.

I don't think that means those jobs disappear, to be clear. What I've seen in software is more that the shape of the job changes. You spend less time typing and more time directing, verifying, deciding what to build. But the point is that the change hits there first and fastest, because that's where the model's native medium and the job's native medium happen to be exactly the same.

r001.rationale: It describes AI models as transforming bits into bits, but does not frame AI as a third kind of manipulator alongside humans and conventional computers.

r002.rationale: It says physical-world work depends on slower, more capital-intensive robotics, while digital work can be changed quickly and is affected first.

r003.rationale: It says digital jobs may change rather than disappear, but does not state that the employment effect could be either an increase or a decrease.

r004.rationale: It does not identify demand elasticity as a factor in AI’s effect on employment.

astra-6.text:
Because the entire workflow is already inside the computer. The inputs are digital, the outputs are digital, and increasingly AI can do the transformation in between. If your work involves reading documents, writing code, analyzing data, or producing reports, you don’t need to solve robotics to start changing that work. You need a system that can operate on information.

The physical world has this additional bottleneck. You need hardware, you need to perceive and manipulate a messy environment, and you have to deal with wear and tear and safety. With digital work, once you have something that works, you can deploy copies of it much more easily.

But I think it’s useful to look at tasks rather than whole professions. A job is a bundle of things, and some of those things will become dramatically cheaper while others still require a person to set direction, supply context, or check the result. So the profession can change substantially before you’d say it’s been automated.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can transform digital information, but does not frame it as a third kind of manipulator alongside humans and conventional computers.

r002.rationale: It contrasts digital work, which AI can change without robotics, with physical work that requires hardware, perception, manipulation, and safety, and says digital systems are easier to deploy.

r003.rationale: The response discusses tasks becoming cheaper and professions changing, but does not say whether employment in those professions will increase or decrease.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify demand elasticity as a factor in AI’s employment effects.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is that, for a lot of these professions, both the inputs and the outputs are already digital. You read documents, look at some data, write an email, produce a report, or write code. All of that can happen inside a computer, which means an AI can potentially participate in the entire workflow. It doesn’t need a robot, it doesn’t need to move around in the physical world, and it doesn’t have to deal with all the complexity that comes with that.

And the interface is often language. We use language to describe what we want, to communicate context, and to deliver the result. So language models fit into those workflows quite naturally.

That doesn’t mean you immediately automate an entire profession. A profession is a bundle of tasks, and some of those tasks are much easier to automate than others. Initially, you might have something that drafts a document or writes a piece of code, and a person reviews it. But as these systems become more capable and reliable, the person can delegate larger pieces of the work. So I’d expect the composition of those jobs to change quite substantially.

r001.rationale: The response says AI can participate in digital workflows, but does not frame AI as a third kind of digital-information manipulator alongside people and conventional computers.

r002.rationale: It explains that digital work avoids robotics and physical-world complexity, but does not predict that transformation of physical-world work will lag behind.

r003.rationale: It predicts substantial changes in job composition, but does not say those changes leave employment growth versus decline undetermined.

r004.rationale: The response does not identify demand elasticity as a factor in AI's employment effects.
